item.title: A Bible-quoting Democrat is threatening the GOP's decades-long grip on Texas
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The words “competitive” and “Texas” don’t often show up side by side when it comes to big elections. No Democrat has won a statewide race in the Lone Star State since 1994, and most of the races within that timespan haven’t been particularly close. But now, Democrats are pinning their hopes of ending their three-decade losing streak in Texas on James Talarico, a 37-year-old state lawmaker who has become one of the party’s breakout stars of the midterms. Talarico first gained national attention in March, when he defeated U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett in a high-profile intraparty primary battle. His Republican opponent is Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who bested longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in an often contentious Republican primary runoff. By fusing progressive politics, a soft-spoken demeanor and unapologetic Christian faith, Talarico has built a broad base of support among Texas voters that has allowed him to maintain a steady — yet small — lead in the polls in the months leading up to Election Day. Forecasters list the race as a toss-up. The outcome could have huge implications for American politics. Democrats' hopes of seizing control of the Senate for the final two years of Trump’s presidency hinge on winning at least a couple of seats in historically deep red states like Texas. A victory for Talarico could also cement his position as a key figure in the Democratic Party’s next generation of leaders. With all that in mind, here’s what to know about where Talarico came from, what he stands for and how strong his chances are of turning the Lone Star State blue. Yahoo Where did Talarico come from? Talarico was born in 1989 in Round Rock, Texas, a suburban city of roughly 120,000 people located about 20 miles north of Austin. His birth name was James Dell Causey. Talarico’s mother, Tamara, left his birth father, whom she has described as an abusive alcoholic, when he was 7 weeks old. At first, the mother and son lived in an empty room at the residential hotel where she worked as a sales assistant. It's a story Talarico likes to tell in his stump speech. “My mom showed me that true love doesn't tolerate abuse,” he says. Tamara later married a sales manager named Mark Talarico. The younger Talarico has been devoted to Christianity since childhood. His grandfather was a Baptist preacher in South Texas, and he still goes to the same church — St. Andrew's Presbyterian in Austin — where he attended Bible camp as a kid. In 2018, Talarico asked his pastor if he should run for office or join the ministry. “If you go into the ministry, you'll have clarity, but you won't have power,” the pastor told him . “If you go into politics, you'll have power but won't have clarity. You'll have to work a lot harder to distinguish good from evil.” Talarico chose politics. He earned a degree in government from the University of Texas at Austin and another in education from Harvard, and worked briefly with Teach for America and an education technology nonprofit, before launching a campaign for the Texas House of Representatives. He won after walking the full length of his district — and discovering, in the process, that he has type 1 diabetes. (He was so woozy he spent five days in the ICU.) Over his four terms in the Republican-dominated Texas House, Talarico has opposed GOP efforts to display the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms, restrict voting rights, redraw the state's congressional map and extend its abortion ban. He has helped pass laws to import cheaper medications from Canada, cap the monthly cost of insulin and prevent police from working with reality shows. He enrolled in seminary to deepen his knowledge of the Biblical stories at the base of his politics, graduating with a master’s degree in theological studies. Talarico wasn't Texas Democrats' first choice for the U.S. Senate; the initial frontrunner was ex-congressman Colin Allred, a former NFL linebacker. But during a May 2025 planning meeting with other leading Texas Democrats, Talarico insisted that he was the man for the job. “I told them the fact that I was new, and different, and had no D.C. connection was a huge advantage,” he told the New Yorker in February. “They were all retreads — which I said lovingly.” Former U.S. Rep. Beto O’Rourke — the Democrats’ 2018 nominee for Senate and 2022 nominee for governor — remembered the exchange differently. “James came in, like, ‘I don't care what you guys are doing with your little huddle. F*** all y'all, I'm doing this,’” O'Rourke told the magazine. “He blew everything up in his excitement to make the case for himself.” Compared to Allred, Talarico had far less name recognition in Texas early in the primary race, but he gained steam by leaning into his comparative advantage: his ability to deliver, in his deep Central Texas voice, plainspoken populist sermons that deemphasize the differences between Republicans and Democrats and push for a more “love thy neighbor” approach to politics — messages that tended to go viral. “The biggest divide in our country is not left versus right; it’s top versus bottom,” Talarico likes to tell his 2.6 million Instagram followers. “Billionaires want us looking left and right at each other so that we’re not looking up at them.” Allred dropped out in December as Crockett — a more confrontational figure — entered the race . Polls suggested that the race between Talarico and Crockett would be extremely close, but Talarico ended up winning the primary by a comfortable margin. Where does Talarico stand on key issues? Congressional reform: Talarico supports term limits for members of Congress and a ban on congressional stock trading. He opposes partisan gerrymandering. He has said the Senate should eliminate its filibuster rule so laws can pass with a simple majority vote. Health care: Talarico calls his approach "Medicare for Y'all." He favors letting nonseniors buy into Medicare or providing another "not-for-profit health care option for every American." Immigration: Talarico favors comprehensive immigration reform that would crack down on criminals; provide a pathway to citizenship for certain others; hold Immigration and Customs Enforcement accountable for abuses; and improve the asylum and guest worker systems. He likes to say that "our border should be like a front porch — it should have a welcome mat out front and a lock on the door." Foreign policy: Talarico supports a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. He has condemned what he called Israel's "war crimes" while describing the conflict itself as "the moral test of our time." He opposes the sale of offensive weapons to Israel and has refused to take money from the pro-Israel lobby group AIPAC . "I think God is screaming at us in Gaza right now," he has said. He has also criticized Trump’s handling of the war with Iran, pledging to help “end the forever war” if he’s elected to the Senate. Taxes: Talarico supports raising taxes on billionaires and corporations, as well as tax cuts for the middle class and the expansion of tax credits for working-class Americans. Can Talarico win Texas in November? There has been no shortage of Democrats trying to turn the Lone Star State blue in recent years. O'Rourke even parlayed his early buzz into a 2020 presidential bid. But the last time Texas actually elected a new Democratic senator was in 1970 , so Talarico has a lot of history to overcome if he hopes to win. Some key things have broken in his favor, though. The public’s view of Trump has declined to the point where even a majority of Texans say they disapprove of his job performance. The far-right Paxton is also widely seen as the more vulnerable of the two Republicans who faced off in the GOP primary. He is a favorite of Trump's MAGA base, but he has also been shadowed by scandal: a suspension from office after being impeached on accusations of abusing his office to help a real estate investor (he was later acquitted by the Texas Senate); a 2015 indictment on securities fraud charges that were dismissed in 2024 ; and a recent divorce filing by his wife, a Republican state senator who accused him of committing adultery. Recent polls have generally shown Talarico with a narrow lead, though some have found the candidates tied or Paxton ahead. Talarico’s chances of victory depend on his ability to consolidate a broad and diverse coalition of Texas voters, many of whom would be supporting a Democrat for the first time. “In Texas, you cannot do this with just Democrats,” political strategist Mike Madrid, a centrist Republican, told Newsweek after Talarico's primary win . “You have to win Republicans. His whole approach has been about building a bigger coalition.” This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/who-is-james-talarico-a-guide-to-the-rising-democratic-star-whos-trying-to-turn-texas-blue-220106601.html

item.title: Flavio Bolsonaro lands in U.S. after fleeing Brazil following election loss
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Flavio Bolsonaro lost elections to Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and refused to concede defeat (Evaristo Sa) Defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro will be granted entry into the United States, Washington said Tuesday, amid media reports that he has left Brazil for the country despite a court order banning his exit. The son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro lost the presidential election Sunday to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and refused to concede defeat. The US State Department said Tuesday it would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them entry into the United States, without confirming his travel plans. The 45-year-old arrived in the United States Tuesday, CNN and the Washington Post reported, each citing an anonymous source. But where he landed remains unknown. The right-wing senator on Monday said a Supreme Court justice had ordered him to hand over his passports. Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity. A police source told AFP that the senator's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, adding that "there is no formal record of Flavio Bolsonaro leaving the country." But he has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document seen by AFP. Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho expressed shock over reports that the defeated candidate had fled Brazil. "We still don't have any news about his whereabouts," he told reporters Tuesday in Brasilia. "I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it," Marinho said. "That was the only communication we had." - 'Shameful' - Lula called fleeing the country a "shameful" act. "A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful," he remarked in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration. Bolsonaro said Monday that the ban on his exit from Brazil amounted to a scare tactic. "I never had any intention of leaving the country," he said in a video posted on Instagram. US President Donald Trump, a close ally of Jair Bolsonaro, on Monday said Brazil's elections were "rigged" following the defeat of Bolsonaro junior. Flavio's brother Eduardo, a US-based former lawmaker, maintains close ties with the White House. Last week, he told a US podcast that Flavio Bolsonaro should leave Brazil in the event of electoral defeat, given the active probes into his activities. In his Monday statement, Lula's challenger also said he would lead the opposition to the leftist government. Following Lula's victory with 51.8 percent of the vote, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transportation difficulties that prevented some citizens from voting. Lula had requested the extension, as had Bolsonaro over bad weather in parts of the country. - In his father's footsteps - All bets were on a Bolsonaro win after he came out on top in the first round of elections earlier this month. He campaigned on a pledge to liberate his father, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later. Separately on Tuesday, the Supreme Court ordered police to investigate alleged foreign funding of Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign and other interference from abroad such as social media "manipulation." Lula's campaign complained about election interference by Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, claiming "algorithmic manipulation." Meta denies taking any actions to favor one side in the election, but previously said that some of Lula's campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors. bur-cc-bys/sla This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/brazils-flavio-bolsonaro-flees-us-220155232.html

High prices that have strained household budgets have become the dominant issue in the election, weighing down Republican candidates in red states such as Texas. Trump on Tuesday defended his decision to attack Iran, saying it was “one of the greatest things I ever did,” and claiming that prices at the pump would fall once the war is over, even with no clear off-ramp to a conflict now in its eighth month. “Short-term pain, right, for long-term gain. You’re going to see very soon,” Trump said at a rally in Corpus Christi. The average price for a gallon of regular was $4.27, according to auto club AAA, up from $2.98 before the war. The president also hailed an oil tanker arriving at the Corpus Christi port from Venezuela, an effort to showcase energy supplies from the Latin American country. He earlier told reporters he would visit the ship. The Trump administration has touted its control over Venezuela’s natural resources after capturing former leader Nicolás Maduro. Earlier: Trump, Rubio Plan to Visit Tanker With Venezuelan Crude in Texas “It’ll be refined right here in Texas, including right here in Corpus Christi,” Trump said at the rally. “And you’ll see, it’ll happen very quickly. It’ll be like a blink. Gasoline and diesel prices will soon come down.” In an effort to mobilize conservative voters in Texas, the president also repeated his attacks on Talarico, including accusations that he is a vegan, opposes gun rights, and supports transgender individuals. “The only man standing between Texas and this raging lunatic is a man named President Donald J. Trump,” Trump said. “And I need the help of Ken Paxton.” With Democrats needing to net only four seats to take control of the Senate, the race in Texas has taken on outsized importance and given them hope of achieving a long-sought goal of turning the state blue. Paxton’s political career includes numerous scandals that have alienated him from fellow party members. Trump endorsed him in the primary contest over incumbent Republican Senator John Cornyn, a conservative who has clashed with the president but likely would have had an easier path to reelection. Trump’s efforts to help Paxton are fueled in part by his desire to keep the Senate in Republican hands and to prove that his backing of a candidate with political baggage did not jeopardize that goal. Trump has been traveling around the country to help candidates in tight races, most of them in politically red states that he had no trouble winning in the 2024 presidential election. But his low approval ratings have given Democrats a shot at winning seats that earlier would have been unthinkable. Texas has not had a Democrat represent it in the Senate in decades. item.title: Alex Pretti's family says the DOJ is stonewalling their efforts for justice
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Michael Pretti and Susan Pretti, parents of Alex Pretti, who was killed by federal immigration agents in January, listen during a news conference, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, in Minneapolis. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt) - Ellen Schmidt/AP The parents of Alex Pretti , a US citizen shot and killed by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, are accusing the Department of Justice of violating their rights under a federal victims’ rights law, as they demand transparency and justice in their son’s death. In a July letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche — obtained exclusively by CNN — an attorney representing Michael and Susan Pretti wrote they have not received any substantive updates from the DOJ regarding an investigation into their son’s death, and called the department’s attitude toward the case “cruel.” “The government’s pattern of conduct is not only unconscionable, but unlawful,” the letter states. Pretti’s parents on Tuesday accused the federal government of “shielding Alex’s killers” by not turning over the entire federal case file to state investigators. “We will no longer stay silent about the actions of the Department of Justice in the 275 days since Alex’s murder,” Pretti’s father, Michael, said in the family’s first news conference since the 37-year-old ICU nurse’s death. The Pretti family met with US Attorney for the District of Minnesota Dan Rosen on July 13, the letter explains, the same day Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced in a news conference federal officials had handed over volumes of evidence from Pretti’s shooting. However, the letter goes on to say that, despite a public acknowledgment from local officials of an evidence-sharing agreement, Rosen refused to provide any information and would not even confirm the arrangement. A gunshot perforation in a window pane can be seen in a window in front of a makeshift memorial for Alex Pretti on January 26 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. - Roberto Schmidt/AFP via Getty Images “It is impossible to convey how the government’s refusal to engage in transparent communication with the Pretti family has compounded their heartbreak,” the missive says. “Further, with each such refusal, U.S. Attorney Rosen even refused to explain the basis for his position, instead stating only that ‘I can’t tell you for all kinds of reasons,’ without providing a single one,” according to the letter. Federal investigators who briefly agreed to share their evidence with state law enforcement have since stopped cooperating , said Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, who is leading a lawsuit against the Department of Justice. “We are in litigation with the federal government right now to secure the rest of the remaining file, which they could give us this morning if they were inclined to do so, but it looks like we’re going to need a court order. I’m sorry that it comes to that,” Ellison told CNN’s Sara Sidner Tuesday morning. “Any prosecutor can tell you, you can’t go forward with half a file. You need the whole thing.” CNN has reached out to the DOJ and the US Attorney for Minnesota. Pretti’s death was captured in its entirety on video. Like some other incidents that occurred as a result of the Trump administration’s ongoing immigration crackdown, the footage from Pretti’s shooting differed from the version of events provided by the Department of Homeland Security. unknown content item - Kristi Noem, then-DHS secretary, initially described Pretti as a “terrorist” who “attacked” officers after “brandishing” a weapon, though the video disputed those claims. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller referred to Pretti as an “assassin” who tried to murder federal agents. “No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex,” Michael Pretti said Tuesday. Video footage shows, minutes before the fatal encounter with Pretti, immigration agents patrolling a Minneapolis street and interacting with bystanders. A witness, Nilson Barahona, told CNN agents were trying to apprehend someone who fled into a donut shop that locked its doors, leaving the group of federal officers on the sidewalk and street. Agents detained one observer as others blew whistles, yelled and recorded video on their phones. Video shows Pretti attempting to intervene in a scuffle between an observer and the agents. During the incident, Pretti was pepper-sprayed in the face. One of the officers can be heard in the footage shouting: “Gun! Gun! Gun!” as Pretti is on his knees and bent forward. An agent removed Pretti’s gun from his waistband and can be seen exiting the skirmish. At about the same time, one agent drew his service weapon. About a second after the agent holding Pretti’s weapon moved away, the officer who drew his own weapon appeared to fire several shots at Pretti before another agent drew his weapon and a shot rang out. The other officer then raised his gun and fired more shots. At least 10 gunshots can be heard on the video. No daughter should have to wake up and know that her only sibling is no longer here.” “What the federal government has taken away from us, from his friends, his family, his colleagues, from his patients, from the patients’ families. They’ve taken away all of that — and it’s reprehensible,” he told Tapper. Susan Pretti said she knew Alex as her son, but the outpouring of support they’ve received from his friends and coworkers has helped her see another side of him. “Every letter and card that we received from his colleagues, telling us who he was, at work … not only helping his patients but his colleagues,” Susan Pretti said, choking up. “You know what that’s like for a parent to hear? It is probably the kindest thing a parent can ever hear about their child.” unknown content item - Michael Pretti said his trust in the government is fading. Those incidents prompted significant protests in Minneapolis and across the country for weeks. Hennepin County prosecutors have fought the DOJ for key evidence in Pretti’s death for months, after federal law enforcement repeatedly threw up blockades to their access. On the day Pretti was killed, the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension attempted to access the scene to launch an investigation but was banned by federal authorities. CNN was on scene the next day when the BCA first accessed the scene on a court order from a state judge. State and local investigators sued the Trump administration in federal court to obtain evidence in Pretti’s killing. After an evidence-sharing agreement between the DOJ and Minnesota investigators was finalized in June, Hennepin County prosecutors received volumes of evidence in Pretti’s shooting. Weeks later, the DOJ abruptly changed course and stopped sharing information, leaving Hennepin County prosecutors unable to access crucial evidence such as the weapons used to shoot Pretti and the firearm Pretti was carrying in his waistband at the time of the altercation, according to court records filed October 13. People pay their respects during a candlelight vigil for Alex Pretti after he was shot and killed earlier in the day on January 24, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. - Brandon Bell/Getty Images/File The letter from Pretti’s parents asks the DOJ to identify the federal employees who shot and killed Pretti, commit to sharing information with state and local investigators, confirm whether the FBI is continuing to investigate Pretti’s murder, and return any items of Pretti’s personal property no longer needed for evidentiary purposes. “No family should have to beg the U.S. government to do its job,” the letter says. “And no government should act with such caprice.” The Pretti family’s attorney declined to say Tuesday whether they would file a suit of their own against the Department of Justice. “The family will avail itself to any and all remedies in its pursuit of justice for Alex,” Schleicher said. item.title: Judge tosses new charges against ex-FBI officials in Hunter Biden case and criticizes DOJ
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Oct. 27 (UPI) -- A federal judge on Tuesday tossed new obstruction charges the Justice Department filed against two former FBI agents accused of lying to Congress about an investigation into Hunter Biden. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia expressed anger at the federal prosecutors who filed the superseding complaint shortly after midnight Tuesday, CBS News reported. The complaints were unsworn and unsigned. "We have never had complaints filed that are unsigned," Faruqui said. "It is inappropriate. It harms the defendants. "I am frustrated that I got it in the middle of the night. But I am much more concerned that it is filed on the public record." Former agents Nikki Flores, 46, and Bradley Benavides, 56, surrendered on arrest warrants Friday that charged them with lying to Congress about their involvement in the Foreign Influence Task Force investigating the Biden family during the 2020 election cycle. They each faced one count of making a false statement. The charges were announced by U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro. "Lying to Congress by anyone strikes at the heart of our democratic system, but when senior FBI agents lie to Congress believing they are above the law, it's time to bring the hammer of justice down on them," Pirro said in a statement on X . "When senior officials entrusted with safeguarding our nation's security choose deception over duty, they undermine the very institutions they swore to uphold." Prosecutors filed the new complaint to the public court docket Tuesday, adding new charges of obstruction and attempted obstruction of a congressional proceeding. Faruqui said the complaint was never reviewed by him to determine if there was probable cause a crime was committed. He said filing a complaint without judicial review was unprecedented and caused him to question the Justice Department's motivations. The magistrate ordered the complaint to be struck from the record and said the Justice Department could try filing new charges using standard procedures. "Everything you're doing is making me more and more concerned," Faruqui told federal prosecutors. "Why today on this one case have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases? It makes it look like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause." Federal prosecutor John Borchert said it was the first time he'd been aware of a criminal complaint being filed in this manner, as well. He said, though, that prosecutors "are not afraid of a probable cause finding." In a court hearing Tuesday, a lawyer for Flores expressed outrage on behalf of the defense team about the unsigned criminal count added hours before the hearing. "The evidence is mounting that this prosecution is about some political football and not the law or the facts in this case," attorney Mary Dohrmann said in court. "What is going on at the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office? In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Flores and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one" the defense team said in a statement, according to CNBC . "In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed. That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself. "Here, the government has taken that power for itself in a desperate attempt to delay our client's right to challenge the charges in court and litigate this case in the media, rather than the courtroom." item.title: Judge rules a top federal prosecutor is 'unlawfully serving' and bars him from cases
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli in June 2025. (Damian Dovarganes / Associated Press) A federal judge on Tuesday ruled that Bill Essayli is unlawfully serving as Los Angeles’ top federal prosecutor and ordered him disqualified from overseeing two criminal cases, rejecting the Justice Department’s latest effort to preserve his authority. Senior U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright, however, delayed the disqualifications from taking effect while he considers an anticipated government request for a stay pending appeal. Although the order applies to two prosecutions, Seabright rejected the legal arrangement that has allowed Essayli to continue leading the office under the title of first assistant U.S. attorney. He concluded that the Justice Department had unlawfully delegated powers so sweeping that Essayli in effect occupied the U.S. attorney’s position. “In sum, Essayli is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney,” Seabright wrote. After learning about Seabright’s ruling from The Times, Essayli on Tuesday afternoon said that his office expected it and that the case “will be decided by the Supreme Court.” In a follow-up email, he said, “I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” H. Dean Steward, a defense attorney who filed a renewed motion in August challenging Essayli’s authority, called the decision “a victory for the rule of law and the U.S. Constitution.” “The Trump administration ignored the laws governing the appointment of U.S. Attorneys and got caught in Los Angeles,” he said in an emailed statement. “Trump and his Department of Justice violated the law again and again in an effort to install minions as chief federal prosecutors.” The dispute is part of a nationwide battle over the Trump administration’s efforts to install its chosen prosecutors without Senate confirmation. Alina Habba stepped down as New Jersey’s top federal prosecutor in December after an appeals court found her appointment unlawful. In Virginia, a judge’s finding that Lindsey Halligan was unlawfully appointed led to the dismissal of indictments against former FBI Director James Comey and New York Atty. Gen. Letitia James. In his Tuesday ruling, Seabright declined to dismiss the indictments against defendants in the two cases that he banned Essayli from overseeing. Jaime Hector Ramirez and Tu Anh Tran had not shown the substantial prejudice required for that relief, he said in response to attorneys’ requests to dismiss the indictments. His order bars Essayli from participating in or supervising their cases, including overseeing the attorneys handling them. Seabright last year ruled that Essayli was “not lawfully serving” as acting U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, but allowed him to continue exercising authority as a special attorney and first assistant U.S. attorney. The new decision follows a U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruling rejecting a similar arrangement for Nevada prosecutor Sigal Chattah. The appellate court ruled that the Department of Justice cannot keep an official who has not been confirmed by the Senate in charge of a U.S. attorney’s office simply by giving that person a different title and the full powers of the job. The Trump administration has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to review the Nevada decision, arguing that federal law allows the attorney general to delegate a vacant office’s powers and install a new first assistant as its acting leader. The Supreme Court has not said whether it will take up the case. The Justice Department sought to address the 9th Circuit ruling through a revised delegation of authority expressly excluding certain powers reserved for a U.S. attorney. At an Oct. 13 hearing, Assistant U.S. Atty. Alexander Robbins argued before Seabright that the revised delegation placed Essayli’s authority on the permissible side of the line drawn by the appeals court. Seabright found that the revision made no meaningful difference because those powers could not have been delegated to Essayli in the first place. “Withholding the three specific statutory powers mentioned in the revised designation order in reality withholds nothing,” Seabright wrote. A former Republican member of the California Assembly from Riverside, Essayli has used his position to act as one of Trump’s fiercest legal foot soldiers. He has pursued criminal charges against protesters, activists and immigrants while dropping cases involving administration allies and supporting lawsuits challenging transgender and environmental policies in California. Essayli was sworn in as interim U.S. attorney in April 2025. Around the time he hit that role’s 120-day limit, he resigned and then-Atty. Gen. Pam Bondi appointed him as a special attorney and designated him first assistant in an attempt to make him acting U.S. attorney. Seabright rejected that maneuver last year. But the judge initially permitted him to supervise prosecutions in his other roles — an arrangement the subsequent 9th Circuit ruling undermined. Trump still had not nominated anyone to serve as U.S. attorney for the Central District of California as of Tuesday’s ruling, Seabright noted. At the Oct. 13 hearing, Robbins said the government would appeal any disqualification ruling and warned of “the chaotic practical effects” of an order taking effect without a stay. Under the schedule accepted by Seabright, prosecutors have five business days after the ruling to seek a stay pending appeal. If he denies that request, the disqualifications would take effect one week later, subject to further orders from him or an appellate court. item.title: Federal prosecutors fail to get grand jury indictment against Cassidy Hutchinson
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Federal prosecutors were rebuffed in their effort to secure an indictment against former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her testimony related to the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the U.S. Capitol, according to four sources briefed on the grand jury proceedings. The Justice Department has not yet responded to a request for comment. The Washington Post first reported that the grand jury declined to indict Hutchinson. The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has been handling the Hutchinson investigation, CBS News previously reported, and during a hearing on another matter Tuesday, a litigator with the division, Neville Hedley, told U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that the grand jury had not concurred on the proposed indictment. Hedley did not say who the defendant was, but multiple sources confirmed it was Hutchinson. Hutchinson, who was a top aide to White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, angered President Trump's allies and his base when she testified in 2022 before the House select committee investigating the 2021 Capitol attack. In depositions and congressional testimony, Hutchinson said that Mr. Trump and Meadows were warned on Jan. 6 that some of his supporters were carrying weapons to the Capitol, but Mr. Trump said he didn't care — and he tried to order officials to remove the magnetometers at the rally where he spoke that morning. She also relayed a story she said had been told to her by then-White House deputy chief of staff Tony Ornato, in which Mr. Trump grew incensed after his lead Secret Service agent would not drive him to the Capitol after the president's speech to supporters. During that address on the White House Ellipse, he had encouraged them to go to the Capitol, where Congress was confirming the Electoral College results from the 2020 election. He told supporters that "after this, we're going to walk down, and I'll be there with you." Hutchinson testified that Ornato had told her that in the car, Mr. Trump lunged at the steering wheel. Her account was later contradicted by Mr. Trump's driver, who in sworn testimony claimed that the president never tried to grab the steering wheel. CBS News could not determine precisely which parts of Hutchinson's testimony were being scrutinized by prosecutors. According to media reports, House Republican allies of the president made the referral to the Justice Department. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/grand-jury-declines-to-indict-trump-critic-cassidy-hutchinson-over-jan-6-testimony/

item.title: 3 Alexander brothers each get 30 years for sex trafficking after women speak in court
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their brother, Alon, listen as their lawyers argue for lesser sentences at a New York courtroom Tuesday. (Jane Rosenberg / Reuters) Two former luxury real estate brokers and their brother were each sentenced to 30 years in federal prison, seven months after they were convicted of drugging and raping women in a sex trafficking ring. Federal prosecutors sought life sentences for Oren and Alon Alexander, a pair of former powerful real estate brokers, and their brother, Tal, in a New York City courtroom Tuesday afternoon. Attorneys for the brothers, who have asserted their innocence, asked the judge to give the men the mandatory minimum, instead. U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni characterized the brothers as “Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.” On one side, they were described as gentlemen who loved their children, she said, and on the other, they were described as “sadistic, misogynistic, sexual predators.” “Your conduct was monstrous,” Caproni said in her sentencing. But Caproni added that she did not believe the Alexander brothers were beyond redemption, declining the request to give them life sentences. In addition to 30 years of incarceration, she ordered 10 years of supervised release and sex offender treatment approved by the probation office. They are not to have contact with any child under age 18 unless it is approved by the probation office. Twins Alon and Oren Alexander, 39, were ordered to pay $300,000 each in fines. Tal Alexander, 40, was ordered to pay $350,000. Caproni said she will ask the Bureau of Prisons to consult with experts about whether they should be allowed to be held together, as she believes they are bad influences on one another. The men were found guilty in March of 10 counts, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking and sex trafficking by force, after a trial that included testimony from 11 women who described being lured, drugged and sexually assaulted over a period of years. Six of the women were part of the indictment. Tal Alexander and Oren Alexander in New York in 2016. (Sean Zanni / Patrick McMullan via Getty file) In a sentencing memo, prosecutors in New York’s Southern District said more than 70 women came forward with allegations of abuse and accused the brothers of exploiting their wealth, influence and connections to target victims. Victim statements from 11 women, some using court-assigned pseudonyms, were read at the hearing before the judge’s decision. The women asked Caproni to impose a sentence that was appropriate for the profound impact the men had on their lives. One victim, Maya Miller, described the trauma of her rape by Tal Alexander as having settled into her nervous system. “I carry a quiet funeral inside me,” Miller said. Another victim, Olivia Lane, told the judge that she was “profoundly incapacitated” after having had a fraction of one drink while meeting Oren Alexander. She described being raped at least a dozen times while she was terrified and in pain. She then directly addressed the men. “You are weak. You are inhumane,” Lane said. “You never had power, and look at you now.” Two women described the men as having almost inhuman eyes during their assaults. Isa Brooks said, “Their eyes went black during the attack, like I was being mauled by animals.” Lane said, “I remember looking at him and seeing a monster, black eyes.” The women also emphasized the Alexander brothers’ lack of remorse or acknowledgment of their victims throughout the trial. Victim Katie Moore noted in her statement that after five weeks of trial and having been found guilty, the men “cannot even look us in the eye as we speak today.” “These men spent years treating women and girls like their humanity meant nothing,” Moore said. The brothers honed their methods together, attacking women in a way that was designed to humiliate and degrade them, prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said at the sentencing. “When they were done, they bragged to each other and their friends. ... The defendants knew exactly what they were doing, and they did it anyway, and they did it over and over and over again,” she said. Oren Alexander, 37, center, and his twin brother, Alon, center-right, speak to their attorney Joel Denaro during their bond hearing at the Richard E. Gerstein Justice Building on Dec. 13, 2024, in Miami. (Matias J. Ocner / Miami Herald via Getty file) At trial, prosecutors said the brothers raped the women after having promised them parties and trips. One woman testified that she lost control of her body after she had a drink with Alon Alexander at a New York City club. When she awoke, she testified, they were naked on a bed. She kept trying to get up, and he kept pushing her back down, she said. When she told him that she didn’t want to have sex with him, she testified, he responded, “‘You already did.’” In a sentencing submission, attorneys for the brothers acknowledged that they sometimes behaved insensitively toward women but categorically denied that any of them had raped or sexually assaulted anyone. At trial, the attorneys described the sex as consensual and said the women were motivated in part by financial gain. “All the stories were rehearsed,” Tal Alexander’s attorney, Deanna Paul, said in her closing argument. “They’re looking for money.” Paul urged the judge to consider giving her client the mandatory minimum of 15 years in prison, saying the verdict has not changed her view of the evidence. She said 15 years is already an extraordinary punishment, so “what would another 20 or 30 years accomplish?” Attorneys for the two other brothers similarly asked Caproni to give the men 15 years. Marc Agnifilo, who represents Oren Alexander, told her the men all stopped their “sexually aggressive” behavior after they met their wives. “All three defendants stopped, and that matters,” Agnifilo said. Each of the brothers was given an opportunity to address the court directly before he was issued his sentence. Oren Alexander was the first to ask Caproni for a lighter sentence. He once again denied the assaults in his comments before he assaulted her that he has built a new life and family. “My son needs me, and I need to be there for him, and I ask your honor to impose the minimum sentence,” he said. Tal Alexander, who was next to speak, expressed regret over his past actions. “The person who stands in court is not the same man as before,” he said, asking Caproni to consider the entirety of his life in the decision. “I wish I showed more maturity,” he said. “I cannot undo moments when I was immature and careless with other people’s feelings. I understand the jury found me guilty, and I know words cannot change that.” The last brother to speak, Alon, insisted that he was innocent and that he had never raped any women. He invoked his two young daughters in asking for the mercy of the court. “I am afraid of being Daddy in the photograph,” he said. Caproni appeared unmoved by their statements, emphasizing that the rapes were not a result of “party culture or hookup culture” as they described. She said it was not enough to rape the women — the brothers sought to humiliate them, she asserted. “That marriage would transform them from sexual predators to normal gentlemen, I disagree,” Caproni said. “Rape is about power. ... Having a girlfriend or a wife doesn’t mean you are not going to rape or humiliate women.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/ex-luxury-real-estate-brokers-brother-sentenced-federal-sex-traffickin-rcna605818
